input: What is the main idea of the Transformer, and how does it differ from earlier sequence transduction models?
expected_output: The Transformer is a sequence transduction model based solely on attention mechanisms. It dispenses entirely with the recurrence and convolutions used by earlier encoder-decoder models, which makes it more parallelizable and quicker to train while giving better translation quality.

input: How many layers do the encoder and the decoder of the base Transformer have?
expected_output: Both the encoder and the decoder are stacks of N = 6 identical layers.

input: What are the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, and what is applied around them?
expected_output: Each encoder layer has a multi-head self-attention sub-layer and a simple position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. A residual connection is placed around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization.

input: What extra sub-layer does the decoder have, and why is masking used in decoder self-attention?
expected_output: The decoder inserts a third sub-layer that performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Self-attention in the decoder is masked, together with offsetting the output embeddings by one position, so that the prediction for position i can depend only on known outputs at positions before i. This preserves the auto-regressive property.

input: What is scaled dot-product attention, and why are the dot products divided by the square root of d_k?
expected_output: Scaled dot-product attention computes softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V, where Q, K and V are the queries, keys and values. The dot products are scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k) because, for large d_k, they grow large in magnitude and push the softmax function into regions with extremely small gradients.

input: How many attention heads does the base model use, and what is the dimension of each head?
expected_output: The base model uses h = 8 parallel attention heads. Each head has dimension d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64, with d_model = 512.

input: Why does the Transformer use multi-head attention instead of a single attention function?
expected_output: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

input: In what three ways is multi-head attention used in the Transformer?
expected_output: First, in encoder-decoder attention layers, the queries come from the previous decoder layer while the keys and values come from the encoder output. Second, the encoder contains self-attention layers where keys, values and queries all come from the previous encoder layer. Third, decoder self-attention layers let each position attend to earlier positions in the decoder, with masking to prevent leftward information flow.

input: How does the Transformer represent the order of words when it has no recurrence or convolution?
expected_output: It adds positional encodings to the input embeddings at the bottom of the encoder and decoder stacks. The encodings use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies. The authors also tried learned positional embeddings and found nearly identical results.

input: What are the model dimension and the feed-forward inner-layer dimension in the base model?
expected_output: The base model has d_model = 512. The position-wise feed-forward network consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between, and its inner layer has dimensionality d_ff = 2048.

input: Which optimizer and learning rate schedule were used to train the Transformer?
expected_output: The Adam optimizer was used with beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.98 and epsilon = 10^-9. The learning rate was increased linearly for the first warmup_steps = 4000 training steps and then decreased proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number.

input: What regularization techniques were used during training?
expected_output: Two techniques were used: residual dropout and label smoothing. Dropout was applied to the output of each sub-layer before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalized, and also to the sums of embeddings and positional encodings, with P_drop = 0.1 for the base model. Label smoothing with epsilon_ls = 0.1 was also used.

input: Which dataset and hardware were used to train the base model, and how long did training take?
expected_output: The models were trained on the WMT 2014 English-German dataset of about 4.5 million sentence pairs, encoded with byte-pair encoding and a shared source-target vocabulary of about 37000 tokens. Training was done on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model was trained for 100,000 steps, about 12 hours, at roughly 0.4 seconds per step.

input: What BLEU score did the big Transformer achieve on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task?
expected_output: The big Transformer reached 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, outperforming the best previously reported models, including ensembles, by more than 2.0 BLEU. The base model scored 27.3 BLEU.

input: Why did the authors choose self-attention over recurrent and convolutional layers, and how do they compare?
expected_output: The authors compared the layer types on three criteria: total computational complexity per layer, the amount of computation that can be parallelized (the minimum number of sequential operations), and the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. A self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequential operations and a maximum path length of O(1), whereas a recurrent layer needs O(n) sequential operations. Self-attention is also faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d.
